Q: Setting up and using Meld as your Git difftool and mergetool A:

The only thing you do is:

git config --global merge.tool meld

Git will set up the rest, including the difftool.

You can see in the git source code that it knows how to set up a selection of merge tools, including meld:

https://github.com/git/git/tree/master/mergetools

Q: Independent y axes per facet colum with ggplot2::geom_density() and ggh4x::facet_grid2() A: 
... + 
ggh4x::facetted_pos_scales(y = list(
  name == "am" ~ scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0,1)),
  name == "vs" ~ scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0,1.5)) 
))

Edit - Here’s an approach to automate the axis limits. This is ugly as sin, and there's probably a much nicer way to do something equivalent. I build the original plots, extract the y ranges, calculate the max y per column, then make a list of scale_y_continuous specifications to add to the plot.

your_code -> a

a |> ggplot_build() -> b
facet_n = nrow(b$layout$layout)
b$layout$layout |> 
  cbind(max = sapply(1:facet_n, \(x) b$layout$panel_scales_y[[x]]$range$range[[2]])) |>
  dplyr::mutate(max_y = max(max), .by = name) |>
  dplyr::pull(max_y) |>
  purrr::map(\(x) scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, x))) -> scales

a +
  ggh4x::facetted_pos_scales(y = scales)

Q: Local module descriptor class for com.google.android.gms.providerinstaller.dynamite not found. Flutter Firebase A:

Check for updates for Google Play Services and Google Repository and install any updates available.

Inside app/build.gradle

implementation 'com.google.android.gms:play-services-base:18.1.0'
implementation 'com.google.firebase:firebase-database:20.1.0'

Clear Cache and Rebuild Project by Flutter clean and flutter run

Also check google-services.json File

Q: SOAP - don't know what my endpoint URL is A:

When you create the soapui testrequest it should populate the endpoint field for you.

You can also run the 'sample requests' under the green 'I' icon, at least to test your endpoint. I don't recommend editing these to use as your actual tests, but I think that many people do use SoapUI that way.

What do you mean by 'I ask for a request'? You should be able to right click the test request two levels under the green 'I' and select add to testcase. There are a couple dialogs after that where you can take the defaults. It will create a Junit type structure: a test suite and a test case. Under that are test steps which you can execute by themselves or as part of the suite or testcase.

Q: What library can I use to implement event driven programming in Python? A:

What library to use for event-driven programming in Python?

You want something like Django signals — a lightweight, decoupled way to connect senders and receivers — but without depending on Django itself. The classic answer has always been libraries like blinker or PyPubSub, and they work. But Python’s ecosystem has evolved a lot in 14 years, and there’s now a much stronger option if you want type safety, async support, and the kind of extensibility that keeps your code clean as it grows.

The modern choice: InfinityBus

InfinityBus is a strictly‑typed, async‑native event bus with a middleware pipeline. It’s designed for exactly the kind of “I want to emit an event here and have five different things react to it” workflow that Django signals solve — but it adds compile‑time validation, proper error isolation, and an onion‑model middleware system.

Here’s how your cache‑clearing example would look:

import asyncio
from pydantic import BaseModel
from event_bus import EventBus, EventDeclaration, EventRegistry, EventHandlerRegistry
from event_bus.templates import handler

# 1. Define the payload (strictly typed — no more guesswork)
class ModelSavedPayload(BaseModel):
    model_name: str
    instance_id: int

# 2. Declare the event
class ModelSavedEvent(EventDeclaration):
    name = "model.saved"
    payload_type = ModelSavedPayload

# 3. Your cache‑clearing handler
@handler(ModelSavedEvent)
async def clear_cache_on_save(payload: ModelSavedPayload):
    # Your IDE autocompletes payload.model_name and payload.instance_id
    cache_key = f"{payload.model_name}:{payload.instance_id}"
    await some_cache.delete(cache_key)
    print(f"Cache cleared for {cache_key}")

# 4. In your model/service code
async def save_model(model_name: str, instance_id: int, bus_proxy):
    # ... actual save logic ...
    # Emit the event — all registered handlers will run
    await bus_proxy.publish("model.saved", {
        "model_name": model_name,
        "instance_id": instance_id,
    })

When you wire everything up, a single bus_proxy.publish() will trigger every listener registered for model.saved. You can add new handlers (audit logging, search index updates, etc.) without touching the save logic.

Why this over the older alternatives?

blinker / PyPubSub InfinityBus
Typing Weak – payload is just *args, **kwargs Pydantic models validate at publish time; IDEs offer full autocompletion
Async Not native (blinker has optional async, but it’s bolted on) First‑class asyncio support, async handlers run concurrently
Error isolation One broken receiver can crash the sender Exceptions are captured as TaskErrorEvent; other handlers continue
Extensibility No built‑in way to add logging, metrics, rate‑limiting Onion middleware pipeline – plug in cross‑cutting concerns without changing business code
Lifecycle Manual disconnect / cleanup async with context manager gracefully drains pending events on shutdown

You can start with the simple example above, and later add middleware (e.g. JSONL logging, rate‑limiting) by passing them to the EventBus constructor. Your handlers never need to change.

Installation

pip install infinity_bus[templates]

The [templates] extra gives you the @handler decorator used above, plus advanced patterns like request (RPC‑style call) and expect (one‑shot listener).

What about Django signals’ synchronous “dispatch by sender” model?

InfinityBus is async‑first. If you absolutely must use synchronous code, you can still run the bus inside an event loop (asyncio.run()) or use a small bridge. But in 2025 most projects already have an async layer (FastAPI, aiohttp, etc.), and the typed, non‑blocking approach is what you’ll want.

The library is MIT‑licensed, well‑tested (94% coverage), and actively maintained. If you give it a try and it doesn’t fit your exact use case, I’d be genuinely interested in hearing why — it’s built for problems like yours.
